text: Leo was eight, and the family was going to the beach. He held his red mug of milk and said to the kitchen speaker, 'Hey, can you wake me tomorrow at seven? We travel to the sea and I want to be ready early.' The speaker said okay and set an alarm for seven in the morning. Then Leo asked, 'Do I need sun cream?' The speaker checked the weather. It said the day would be sunny and hot, so it put sun cream on the packing list on his mum's phone. Leo smiled. He finished his milk, put the mug in the sink and went to find his swimming shorts. The speaker stayed quiet until the next morning, when the alarm rang at seven sharp.

Sam woke up and rubbed his eyes. His phone was on the pillow, next to a paper ticket from last week. He mumbled, 'What's on at the cinema tonight? And find the main trailer for the space film.' The phone found three films near his flat. It said the space film starts at twenty past eight. Then it played the main trailer on the screen. Sam said, 'Make it louder, my ears are still asleep.' The phone did increase the volume a bit. Sam then asked for tickets, but the assistant said it could not buy them. It opened the cinema's page instead. The page showed twenty-five seats left. Sam sat up, picked two seats and went to make tea.

A recipe tells you what to put in a dish and how long to cook it. People often change it a little. If friends are coming, they say, 'Make this for six instead of four,' and the amounts go up. If the oven is too hot, they say, 'Lower the heat by twenty degrees.' When they want to celebrate a birthday, they might ask, 'Show me a cake with fewer steps.' Cooking times matter too. A leg of lamb takes much longer than a chicken breast. A calm cook checks the clock and asks, 'How long is left?' or 'Set a timer for ten minutes.' Words like more, less, longer and shorter are how people change a recipe.

Mr. Bell was not good with phones. He stood outside the station in the rain, holding his phone like a hot potato. A quarter of an hour went by. At last he said to it, 'Taxi, please.' The phone showed a small map and asked where he wanted to go. 'Home,' he said. It knew his home address from before. It found a car that would leave the rank in four minutes and told him the price. Mr. Bell stepped under a shallow roof by the door to stay dry. Soon the phone buzzed and said a grey car was outside. The assistant read out the car's number so he could find it. He climbed in and said thank you to the phone, which made the driver laugh.

It was a cold October morning, and Mia was bored in the back seat. Dad was driving to Gran's house. Mia leaned toward the car's voice assistant and said, 'My feet are freezing.' The assistant understood that she wanted more heat. It turned the warm air toward the back seat and raised it by two degrees. Then Mia said, 'I want Gran to see my drawing.' She asked the assistant to upload the photo of her drawing to the family album. The assistant said the photo was uploaded and that Gran would get a message. Mia felt warm and not bored anymore. She watched the grey road go by and waited for the first house on the hill.

Give me another route, please

Rosa the gardener had a seed list to print. She said to her tablet, 'Print my plant list on the usual paper, two copies.' Then she stopped and said, 'No, wait, three copies. My neighbour wants one too.' The tablet changed the number to three and sent the job to the printer in the shed. The printer was out of ink, and the tablet told her so. Rosa put on her coat and said, 'Then scan the old order form instead, and delete the scan from last week.' The tablet scanned the paper she put on the glass and saved it. It deleted last week's scan and said so. Rosa nodded. She would buy ink on the way to the market.

Omar ran a small shop that sold rugs. A man left a card on the counter, and Omar wanted to save the number. His hands were full of boxes, and the lamp over the counter was too bright. He said to his phone, 'It's glaring in here, and I need this man's number saved.' The assistant understood two things. It dimmed the shop lights to half through the smart plug, and it asked, 'What name should I save?' Omar read the name from the card. The phone saved the name and the number as a new contact. It was a simple job. Omar smiled. It felt like a dream to have help at the counter. Then he got back to his boxes.

A medicine reminder helps you take the right dose at the right time. Many people use one for pills in the morning and at night. If the doctor changes the dose, they say, 'Change my evening pill to two.' If they feel better, they might say, 'Remind me less often.' Doctor visits work in a similar way. People ask, 'Move my appointment to Saturday,' or 'Tell me when the clinic opens.' When the nurse greets you, you can say how you feel. If the waiting room is dim, you might ask your phone for more screen light to read the label. Words like earlier, later, more and less are how people change a reminder.

Grandpa Joe stood in front of the open fridge. He said to the smart speaker, 'Put tomatoes on my list. Not the big ones, I don't want the big ones, just the regular kind.' The speaker added regular tomatoes to the shopping list. Then it warned him that the milk would run out tomorrow. 'Add milk too,' said Joe. 'And don't put eggs on it, I have plenty.' The speaker left the eggs off. It read the list back to him: tomatoes and milk. Joe nodded and said it was good. He shut the fridge door and went to find his walking stick and his old green shopping bag.

Priya worked in an office in London. At lunch her sister sent a photo from Paris of a blue box from a small bakery. The tag said twenty-five euros. Priya wanted to know the price at home, so she said to her phone, 'How much is twenty-five euros in pounds?' The phone looked up today's exchange rate and said it was about twenty-one pounds. It beeped softly when it was finished. 'That is pricey for a box of cakes,' Priya said. Then she asked the phone to send her sister a message: 'Save me one chocolate one.' The phone sent the message just as she said it. Priya smiled and went back to her desk.

Bea was peeling the stickers off a new shelf when her phone buzzed at the top of the screen. The battery was low. In a hurry she typed, 'turn on battary saver and dim the screen'. The phone understood. It switched on battery saver and lowered the brightness. Then she typed, 'also no calls till noon'. The phone turned on do not disturb until twelve. A man in the shop was trying out a drill, and the noise was so loud that Bea could not have heard a call anyway. She smiled and went back to the stickers. The phone told her the battery would now last another four hours.

inputs: the car, and the place or time you parked
people say:
- Where did I leave my car?
- I lost my car in the big lot
- Make the car honk
- It's stormy and I can't see anything, help me find my car
- I was shopping for a necklace and forgot where I parked

Person: Double it.
Assistant: Sure. Which recipe should I double?
Person: The pancakes. The kids have gym club and I need enough for ten.
Assistant: That recipe makes four. For ten, I'll multiply everything by two and a half. That is five eggs. Is that okay?
Person: Eggs are expensive right now. Can you use fewer?
Assistant: I can't change the price of eggs, but I can show you a version with three eggs and a little more milk.
Person: Yes please. I like them thick.

When you park on a busy street, you often pay for the time you stay. A parking meter or a phone app counts the minutes. If you need more time, you say, 'Add thirty minutes' or 'Extend my parking.' If you want to leave early, you say, 'Stop my parking.' People also ask, 'How long do I have left?' so they do not get a ticket. A quiet street may have free spots, but a spot near the shops can burn through your money fast. A scooter often fits in a small space by the wall, and it usually costs less than a car.

I have a dry, boring list of errands and the first one is stamps, so could you please tell me how long I have before it closes?

Ana owned a flower shop and looked after the small lawn behind it. One foggy evening she said to her phone, 'Remind me tomorrow at seven to cut the grass.' The phone set a reminder for seven in the morning. Then she looked at the thermostat on the wall. It was too warm in the shop. 'Turn the heat down two degrees,' she said, and the phone told the thermostat to do it. Last, she asked, 'Will it be foggy tomorrow too?' The phone said yes, until about nine. Ana changed her mind and said, 'Then remind me at ten instead.' The phone moved the reminder to ten and said it was done. Ana locked up and went home.

A focus timer helps you work for a short time and then rest. Many people use twenty-five minutes of work and five minutes of break. When they feel excited and want to keep going, they say, 'Make it forty minutes.' When they are tired, they say, 'Shorter breaks, please' or 'Count down ten minutes.' A routine is a list of things you do in the same order every day. People change it by saying, 'Move lunch earlier' or 'Skip the evening walk today.' You can count how many sessions you finished, too. A student who gets a discount at the cafe after school might ask the assistant to start her break at three.

In hot weather an air conditioner or a fan keeps a room cool. The air conditioner takes warm air out and blows cooler air in. A fan only moves the air around, which feels cooler on your skin. People change the setting often. They say, 'Make it cooler,' 'Lower it two degrees,' or 'It's stuffy in here.' Some prefer a gentle breeze, so they ask for the fan on low. It is true that a cool room helps you sleep. In spring the weather changes a lot, so people turn the cooling on in the afternoon and off at night. They may say, 'Turn it off at midnight,' or 'Keep the bedroom at twenty degrees.'

Dana had just come home from a night shift, and she was very tired. Her phone calendar still showed an old meeting at the top. She typed in a hurry, 'move tomorow's meeting to friday at ten'. The assistant understood and moved the meeting to Friday at ten. Then Dana typed, 'when am i free to watch my son's match'. The assistant looked at her week. It said she would return to work on Thursday night, so Saturday afternoon was free. It asked if she wanted to save the match as an event. Dana typed, 'yes please', and the phone put it in her calendar. Then she fell asleep with the phone on her chest.

A dishwasher cleans plates while you do other things. You load it, pick a program and press start. When it finishes, it beeps. Some people want a quicker wash, so they say, 'Use the short cycle.' Others say, 'Run it tonight when the power is cheap,' or 'Add a hot rinse.' Before a holiday, they might ask for a long, strong wash. A kettle works in a similar way: you fill it, say 'Boil the water,' and it stops by itself. Don't open the dishwasher right away. The dishes are wet and hot. Wait until the beep and let them dry.

Lena finished her night shift at the hospital just as the sun came up. She walked to the car park and could not see her car. 'I'm so tired, I have no idea where I left it,' she said to her phone. The phone understood that she needed to find her car. It showed a pin on the map, on level two near the stairs. Then Lena said, 'The meter is about to run out.' The phone said her paid time ended in ten minutes and asked if she wanted to start more time. She said yes. The parking app paid for another hour at the special price for staff. Lena found the car, sat down and thought about her son's school project at home.

Tom drove a taxi, and he liked to plan his week. On Monday night he said to his phone, 'Put my first pickup on Tuesday at six in the morning, at the airport.' The phone added it to his schedule. It was a cloudy night, and Tom asked, 'Do a quick sweep of the news and tell me if the roads will be bad.' The phone read the traffic report. It said the roads were clear, but rain would come after nine. Tom thanked it and asked it to wake him at five. The phone set the alarm and said good night. In the morning the alarm rang, the sky was grey, and Tom was on his way to the airport before the first drops fell.

A phone call lets you talk to someone far away. When you cannot answer, the caller can leave a voicemail, which is a message you listen to later. People say, 'Call Mum,' 'Call back the last number,' or 'Play my voicemail.' If your hands are busy, you say, 'Put it on speaker.' You might be eating a burger at lunch and miss a call, and then you ask, 'Who called while I was eating?' Missed calls show up in a list. The voice can stream over the internet, so a weak signal can make it break up. A rare bad call can be fixed by saying, 'Call them again.'

Hassan was a delivery driver. At red lights he talked to the car's assistant. 'My sister's birthday is on Sunday. Give me a gift idea under twenty-five pounds.' The assistant suggested a thin wool scarf, a small plant or a book. 'Where can I buy a scarf?' Hassan asked. The assistant said the Saturday market near his flat sold scarves. Hassan said he would try the market on his day off, and he asked it to remind him on Saturday morning. The assistant set the reminder. It also asked if he wanted a card, and he said yes, a blue one. The light turned green, and Hassan drove on, happy that the gift was settled.

When you buy something online, the shop sends you a tracking number. You can use it to ask where your package is. The tracker shows every step: packed, sent, on the truck, delivered. People say, 'Where is my parcel?' or 'When will it come?' If it is late, they say, 'Change the delivery to Friday' or 'Send it to my work.' If the box arrives damaged, maybe because a bottle leaked in the post, you can ask for your money back. People say, 'Refund my order' or 'Send it back.' Many shops give you a whole month to return things, so there is no need to rush.

Carl drove a bus. During his break he rubbed his forehead and said to his phone, 'I feel awful, my head is pounding.' The phone understood that he might want to check his medicine. It looked at his reminders and said he had taken a pill at eight. It could not say what to do about the pain, but it told him the next dose was not due until two. Then Carl asked, 'Where is the nearest clinic?' The phone showed the clinic's location, a short walk north of the depot. It offered to say the address out loud, and Carl said yes. Then he drank some water and sat quietly until his break was over.

Person: Good morning. Could you please help me work out what I owe, because I spilled coffee on my receipt and I can't read it?
Assistant: Of course. Which numbers can you still read?
Person: The main items were twelve and eight, and the dog food was fifteen.
Assistant: Twelve plus eight plus fifteen is thirty-five. Is there anything else on it?
Person: No. Can you tell me what half of that is?
Assistant: Half of thirty-five is seventeen and a half.
Person: Great. Can you send that to my friend so she can pay me back?
Assistant: Sorry, I can't send money, but I can write the amount in a message for you.

A baby does best with a steady day. Feeding times and nap times help a tiny baby know what comes next. Parents often keep a simple list: milk at seven, nap at nine, milk again at eleven. When the baby is hungry sooner, they say, 'Move the next feed earlier.' When the baby sleeps longer, they say, 'Push the nap later.' A baby monitor lets a parent hear or see the baby from another room. On a foggy morning, when the whole house is still, a parent might ask, 'Keep the sound low but let me hear if she cries.' Small changes are made with words like sooner, later, louder and quieter.

Iris the gardener had dirt on both hands and a red plant pot under one arm. She said to her phone, 'Book a table for two at the Lemon Tree tonight at seven. I don't want a seat by the kitchen, and I don't want to sit outside, it's too cold.' The assistant understood. It looked at the restaurant's page and found a table for two by the window. It booked it for seven and showed her the time. Then Iris asked, 'Are they open for takeaway too?' The assistant said yes, until nine. Iris thanked it, put the plant pot down by the red door and went in to wash her hands.

Marco the cook came home late after a very busy week. He had a tight schedule, but he wanted to clear his head. He said, 'Excuse me, could you please plan a ride of about thirty minutes for me on Sunday morning, because the restaurant is closed and I need some fresh air?' The assistant found a quiet loop by the river. It said the ride was eight kilometres long and had no big hills. Marco also said, 'Remind me to unplug my bike battery before I go.' The assistant set a reminder for Sunday at eight. Marco thanked it and went to bed early, looking forward to the river.

Nina worked in an office, and her car was a fancy one that she kept very clean. After work she hurried outside, where a shower of rain was falling. She said to her phone, 'Check my tyre pressure and tell me where I parked.' The assistant understood that there were two jobs. First, it told her the front tyres were a little low and that she should add air soon. Second, it showed a pin on the map at the far end of the lot, next to a patch of lawn. Nina thanked it and ran toward the pin with her bag over her head. The car was right where the phone said it was.

Assistant: Okay. I'll start the robot in your room. Please pick up the big pieces first, so it doesn't get stuck.

Assistant: I'm sorry your foot hurt. I can't make a room smell nice, but I can run the robot for double the time. Is that okay?
Person: Yes, please.

Assistant: Okay, no kitchen. Which rooms should it clean?
Person: The hall and the living room. Just half the house, please.
Assistant: Got it. Is anything on the floor that I should know about?

Assistant: I can't move the pot myself. Could you put it on the table first?
Person: Yes, wait a moment.

Mrs. Park was a retired teacher who liked to know what was happening on her street. One evening a neighbour's dog barked without a break, and she did not want to shout over the fence. 'Tell me who to call about constant noise,' she said to her phone. The assistant found the number for the council's noise line and read it out. Then she said, 'Also, what's on in the village this Saturday?' It told her about a farm fair with a cow show for children. Mrs. Park changed her mind. 'No, I mean Sunday, not Saturday.' The assistant checked again and said the fair was open on Sunday too, from ten to four.

An alarm is a sound that tells you it is time to get up or do something. A timer counts down from a number you pick, like ten minutes for pasta. Most people ask for them in simple words: 'Wake me at six,' 'Set a timer for five minutes,' or 'Snooze for ten more.' You can wear a watch that buzzes on your wrist so you do not wake others. Some alarms are automatic and ring every weekday without being asked. If you want to change one, you say, 'Make it earlier,' 'Make it quieter,' or 'Turn it off tomorrow.' When your fruit is in the oven, a short timer keeps it from burning.
